### Effect size with retrospective power analysis {#sec-l06-retrospective}

Reporting the effect size for each estimate (each hypothesis) in the Results section is the norm. With the General Linear Model, the effect size of each estimate is the corresponding standardised estimate $\beta$. Therefore, no other information needs to be reported.

However, you will see a lot of different metrics in research papers using different statistical tests for their hypotheses. Here is a list of the most used:

- Cohen's $d$ for a main effect in a model with 1 categorical predictor with 2 categories
- Eta-squared $\eta^2$ or partial eta-squared $\eta^2_p$ for all the other models

::: {.callout-note title="Note"}
- The $\eta^2_p$ for a particular estimate corresponds to the effect size when the other effects in the model are deliberately ignored.
- Both $\omega^2$ and $\epsilon^2$ (and their partial counterparts, $\omega^2_p$ and $\epsilon^2_p$) are unbiased estimators of the population's $\eta^2$ (or $\eta^2_p$, respectively), which is especially important in small samples.
- $\eta^2_p$ aims at estimating the effect size in a design where all the variables have been experimentally manipulated (e.g., experimental groups). However, some predictors can only be observed. For such cases, we can use generalised eta squared $\eta^2_G$.
:::

## Reasonable statistics {#sec-l06-reasonable}

### Bad versus good science {#sec-l06-badgood}

**$p$-hacking.** Running statistical tests until finding a significant $p$-value is $p$-hacking. To avoid it, all the hypotheses should be tested with one unique test and not with one test by hypothesis. Ideally if another statistical test has to be run, it should be done on new data.

Why does $p$-hacking work? Each test has a 5% risk of a false positive when $H_0$ is true. With several tests, the risk that at least one of them is significant by chance adds up: it is $1 - 0.95^k$ for $k$ independent tests. @fig-l06-false-positives shows that this risk passes 50% at `r min(which(1 - 0.95^(1:20) > 0.5))` tests.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l06-false-positives
#| fig-cap: "The probability of at least one false positive, $1 - 0.95^k$, against the number $k$ of independent tests when every null hypothesis is true."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart with points of the probability of at least one false positive, from 0% to 75%, against the number of tests, from 1 to 20. The red curve starts at 5% for one test, marked by a grey dashed line, and rises steadily. An orange point at 20 tests is labelled 64%."
#| fig-height: 3.2
false_positives <- tibble(tests = 1:20) |>
  mutate(probability = 1 - 0.95^tests)

twenty_tests <- false_positives |>
  filter(tests == 20)

ggplot(false_positives, aes(tests, probability)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, colour = book_col("grey"), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = book_col("red"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  geom_point(data = twenty_tests, colour = book_col("orange"), size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 19.6, y = twenty_tests$probability + 0.05, hjust = 1, size = 3.5, label = paste0("20 tests: ", scales::percent(twenty_tests$probability, accuracy = 1))) +
  annotate("text", x = 20, y = 0.09, hjust = 1, size = 3.4, label = "5% for one test") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.75), labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Number of tests", y = "Probability of at least\none false positive")
```

**$p$-HARKing.** $p$-HARKing (Hypothesising After the Results are Known) is defined as presenting a post hoc hypothesis (i.e., one based on or informed by one's results) in one's research report as if it were, in fact, an a priori hypothesis.

@fig-l06-harking compares the order of the steps in honest research and in $p$-HARKing. Both end with a report of the hypothesis, but in $p$-HARKing the hypothesis is written after the results.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l06-harking
#| fig-cap: "The order of the steps in honest research (top) and in HARKing (bottom)."
#| fig-alt: "Two rows of four boxes joined by arrows. Honest research: Hypothesis, written before the data; Data, collected to test it; Test, one model for all hypotheses; Report, the hypothesis as planned. HARKing: Data, collected first; Tests, many models are tried; Hypothesis, written after the results; Report, presented as if written before."
#| fig-height: 2.9
honest_research <- tribble(
  ~step,        ~detail,
  "Hypothesis", "written\nbefore the data",
  "Data",       "collected\nto test it",
  "Test",       "one model\nfor all hypotheses",
  "Report",     "the hypothesis\nas planned"
)

harking <- tribble(
  ~step,        ~detail,
  "Data",       "collected\nfirst",
  "Tests",      "many models\nare tried",
  "Hypothesis", "written after\nthe results",
  "Report",     "presented as if\nwritten before"
)

(flow_chart(honest_research) + labs(title = "Honest research")) /
  (flow_chart(harking) + labs(title = "HARKing"))
```

**Pre-registration and open science.** In order to avoid any kind of $p$-hacking or $p$-HARKing, research pre-registration is now possible with the open science framework (<https://osf.io/>). Some journals are also encouraging the publication of the data treatment code and all the data sources to replicate the results.

## Agentic AI for statistical analysis {#sec-l06-agentic}

### What about AI? {#sec-l06-whatai}

Traditional AI assistants (like ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude) respond to text prompts: you describe what you want and the AI generates text or code in return. Give them your hypotheses and your data, and they will run the calculation and print out a good quality results section!

Now, you need to supervise and check for misunderstanding (e.g., have the hypotheses been tested in the same model? Are the confidence intervals reported?).

**The issue is transparency!**

### What is agentic AI? {#sec-l06-agentic-ai}

**Agentic AI** goes one step further: it can **interact directly with software on your behalf**. Instead of just telling you what to do, it can click buttons, fill forms, navigate menus, and read results from your screen.

For example, **Claude in Chrome** is a browser extension that allows Claude to click buttons and navigate menus as well as read outputs and interpret results. This means Claude can operate **jamovi Cloud** (<https://cloud.jamovi.org>) directly in your browser!

### Claude in Chrome and jamovi Cloud {#sec-l06-claude-chrome}

::: {.callout-tip .box-howto title="In jamovi Cloud: an analysis with Claude in Chrome"}
Here is how it works:

1. Install the **Claude in Chrome** extension from the Chrome Web Store
2. Open **jamovi Cloud** at <https://cloud.jamovi.org> in a Chrome tab
3. Open the Claude side panel and describe your analysis task
4. Claude navigates jamovi's menus, sets options, and runs the analysis for you
:::

What you can ask Claude to do, for example:

- "Upload this dataset and run a linear regression predicting js_score from salary"
- "Check all the assumption boxes for this regression"
- "Run a correlation matrix for these variables"

::: {.callout-important title="Important caveats"}
<!-- check: availability (beta, paid plans only) and the jamovi Cloud guest plan limits are time-sensitive, confirm they are still current -->
- Claude in Chrome is in **beta** and available on **paid plans only**
- Always **review the results**
- Claude cannot bypass login pages or CAPTCHAs, you must handle those yourself
- jamovi Cloud has **limits** on the free guest plan (e.g., 100 columns, 16 MB file size)
- **Never share sensitive data** without understanding the privacy implications of both jamovi Cloud and Claude in Chrome
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-demo title="Live demonstration"}
In the lecture, Claude in Chrome is demonstrated live on jamovi Cloud. <!-- check: the slide is a bare "Live Demo" divider; what is shown is inferred from the Claude in Chrome and jamovi Cloud slide before it -->
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Always more homework"}
For the next lecture (@sec-lecture-07), read Chapter 12 of "Learning Statistics with jamovi" from <https://www.learnstatswithjamovi.com/>.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-keypoints title="Key points"}
- The General Linear Model has four requirements: linearity of the effects, independence of observations, and normality and equal variance of the residuals. They are never perfectly met, so we check that they are reasonable enough.
- In jamovi, tick all the Assumption Checks: the Q-Q plot of residuals checks normality and the residual plots check equal variance. Independence is a matter of self-assessment, based on how the data were collected.
- Predictors should not be too strongly correlated (a VIF cut-off of 5 is commonly used). No observation should be too influential (a Cook's distance greater than 1 is considered large). An outlier is a cue to look more closely at a case, not a reason to throw it away.
- A model comparison tests whether a variable is useful by comparing a full model with a simple model. It uses the $AIC$ (the smaller, the better) and the $p$-value of the comparison.
- A prospective power analysis gives the sample size needed for a given alpha, a power of at least 0.8 and an expected effect size. In the General Linear Model, the effect size of each estimate is the standardised estimate $\beta$.
- To avoid $p$-hacking and $p$-HARKing, test all the hypotheses with one test, use new data for any other test, and pre-register the research.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-l06-exercises}

These exercises use the Organisation Beta data (`organisation_beta.csv`) and the figures and tables of this chapter. Try each one before opening its solution. Exercises 6 and 7 need jamovi or R.

::: {#exr-l06-vocabulary}
## True or false?

Say whether each statement is true or false, and correct the false ones.

a. The initials of the four requirements of the General Linear Model spell LINE.
b. The outcome variable of a linear regression must be normally distributed.
c. The independence of observations is checked with a box of the Assumption Checks of jamovi.
d. A VIF of 7 suggests that a predictor is too strongly correlated with the other predictors.
e. An observation with a large studentised residual must be removed from the data.
f. Statistical power is the probability of rejecting $H_0$ when $H_a$ is true.
g. A Type I error is failing to reject $H_0$ when $H_a$ is true.
h. When two models are compared, the model with the larger $AIC$ is the better one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
a. True: Linearity (of the effects), Independence (of observations), Normality (of the residuals) and Equal variance (of the residuals).
b. False. The residuals must be normally distributed. The predictors and the outcome can be non-normal.
c. False. Independence is a matter of self-assessment: you need to know how the data were collected. The Autocorrelation test of jamovi only checks whether observations that follow each other in the file are related, which is one kind of dependence among others.
d. True. A cut-off value of 5 is commonly used.
e. False. An outlier is a cue to look more closely at the case. It is removed only if it turns out to be junk data, for example a value recorded incorrectly.
f. True. It is the probability of a True Positive, 1 minus the probability of a Type II error.
g. False. This is a Type II error (False Negative). A Type I error is rejecting $H_0$ when, in fact, $H_a$ is false (False Positive).
h. False. The smaller the $AIC$, the better the model.
:::

@fig-l06-exercise-plots shows four plots drawn from simulated data, as you could see them when you check the assumptions of four different models. It is used in @exr-l06-diagnostics.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l06-exercise-plots
#| fig-cap: "Four plots to check the assumptions of four models fitted to simulated data, for @exr-l06-diagnostics."
#| fig-alt: "Four plots labelled A to D. A: a scatterplot of an outcome against a predictor, with points that rise and then fall in an arch, and a straight blue regression line through them. B: a Q-Q plot of residuals whose points form a curve above the blue line at both ends. C: residuals against fitted values, close to 0 on the left and widely spread on the right. D: residuals against fitted values, a band of the same height everywhere."
#| fig-height: 5.6
exercise_data <- with_seed(6063, {
  predictor_a <- runif(80, min = 0, max = 10)
  fitted_c <- runif(80, min = 2, max = 10)
  fitted_d <- runif(80, min = 2, max = 10)
  list(
    a = tibble(predictor = predictor_a, outcome = 2 + 1.6 * predictor_a - 0.17 * predictor_a^2 + rnorm(80, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)),
    b = tibble(residual = rexp(80) - 1),
    c = tibble(fitted = fitted_c, residual = rnorm(80, mean = 0, sd = 0.15 * fitted_c^1.2)),
    d = tibble(fitted = fitted_d, residual = rnorm(80, mean = 0, sd = 1))
  )
})

plot_a <- ggplot(exercise_data$a, aes(predictor, outcome)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "A", x = "Predictor", y = "Outcome")

plot_b <- ggplot(exercise_data$b, aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = book_col("blue"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  stat_qq(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "B", x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Residuals")

plot_c <- ggplot(exercise_data$c, aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = book_col("grey"), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "C", x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")

plot_d <- ggplot(exercise_data$d, aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = book_col("grey"), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "D", x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")

(plot_a + plot_b) / (plot_c + plot_d)
```

::: {#exr-l06-diagnostics}
## Reading the plots of the assumption checks

Look at @fig-l06-exercise-plots.

1. For each plot, A to D, name the assumption that it checks.
2. For each plot, say whether the assumption is met.
3. Which of the four assumptions cannot be checked with a plot? How do you check it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Questions 1 and 2:

- **A** checks the **linearity** of the effect. The points rise and then fall in an arch, and the straight line misses them at both ends and in the middle: the assumption is not met.
- **B** is a Q-Q plot of residuals, which checks the **normality** of the residuals. The points form a curve and leave the line at both ends: the residuals are skewed, and the assumption is not met.
- **C** is a residual plot, which checks the **equal variance** of the residuals. The spread of the residuals grows with the fitted values, a funnel shape: the assumption is not met.
- **D** is also a residual plot. It shows only a cloud of points with the same spread everywhere: the equal variance assumption is met.

Question 3: the **independence** of observations. It is checked by self-assessment: ask how the data were collected and whether two observations could be artificially related, for example two partners of the same couple.
:::

```{r}
#| label: exercise-anomalous-data
#| include: false
# VIF of the two predictors of the model js_score ~ salary + perf, calculated by hand.
r2_salary_on_perf <- summary(lm(salary ~ perf, data = organisation_beta))$r.squared
vif_additive <- 1 / (1 - r2_salary_on_perf)

cook_additive <- cooks.distance(model_additive)
studentised_additive <- rstudent(model_additive)
employee_largest_cook <- organisation_beta$employee[which.max(cook_additive)]
employee_largest_studentised <- organisation_beta$employee[which.max(abs(studentised_additive))]

# Tolerance of Height in the iqsize model (see the Example on the VIF of Height).
tolerance_height <- 1 - r2_height
```

::: {#exr-l06-vif-cook}
## Reading the VIF and Cook's distance

The model $js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,salary + b_{2}\,perf + e$ is tested on the 20 employees of Organisation Beta. The checks give the values below: the VIF and the tolerance of each predictor, a summary of the Cook's distances and the range of the studentised residuals.

```{r}
#| label: exercise-anomalous-table
tibble(
  Predictor = c("salary", "perf"),
  VIF = format_number(c(vif_additive, vif_additive)),
  Tolerance = format_number(c(1 / vif_additive, 1 / vif_additive))
) |>
  kable(align = "lcc")

tibble(
  Mean = format_number(mean(cook_additive)),
  Median = format_number(median(cook_additive)),
  SD = format_number(sd(cook_additive)),
  Min = format_number(min(cook_additive)),
  Max = format_number(max(cook_additive))
) |>
  kable(align = "c")

tibble(
  `Smallest studentised residual` = format_number(min(studentised_additive)),
  `Largest studentised residual` = format_number(max(studentised_additive))
) |>
  kable(align = "c")
```

1. Is the correlation between $salary$ and $perf$ a problem for this model?
2. Why do $salary$ and $perf$ have the same VIF?
3. Does any employee have a high influence on the model?
4. Is there any outlier, according to the rule of the "Your turn" box on anomalous data?
5. In @tbl-l06-vif, the tolerance of Height is `r format_number(tolerance_height)`. What share of the variance of Height is explained by Brain and Weight?
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. No. The VIF is `r format_number(vif_additive)`, very close to 1 and far below the cut-off value of 5: the two predictors are almost uncorrelated ($r = `r format_number(cor(organisation_beta$salary, organisation_beta$perf))`$).
2. With two predictors, the "other predictors" of each one are only the other one. Both VIFs come from the same $R^2_j$, the square of the correlation between $salary$ and $perf$: $VIF = 1 / (1 - `r format_number(r2_salary_on_perf, 4)`) = `r format_number(vif_additive)`$.
3. No. The maximum Cook's distance is `r format_number(max(cook_additive))` (employee `r employee_largest_cook`), far below 1, and the mean is `r format_number(mean(cook_additive))`.
4. No. The studentised residuals go from `r format_number(min(studentised_additive))` to `r format_number(max(studentised_additive))`, so none is beyond +3 or -3. Employee `r employee_largest_studentised`, at `r format_number(studentised_additive[which.max(abs(studentised_additive))])`, is close to the limit and worth a closer look.
5. The tolerance is $1 - R^2_j$, so $R^2_j = 1 - `r format_number(tolerance_height)` = `r format_number(r2_height)`$: Brain and Weight explain `r scales::percent(r2_height, accuracy = 1)` of the variance of Height.
:::

```{r}
#| label: exercise-power
#| include: false
power_20_per_group <- power.t.test(n = 20, delta = 0.5, sd = 1, sig.level = 0.05)$power
```

::: {#exr-l06-power}
## Reading a power analysis

Use @fig-l06-power-curves and the rules of @sec-l06-prospective.

1. About how many participants per group are needed to detect a large effect ($d = 0.8$) with a power of 0.8? How many in total?
2. A student plans to compare two groups of 20 participants and expects a medium effect ($d = 0.5$). Read the power of this study on the figure. What do you advise?
3. What is the Numerator df of the model $js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,gender + b_{2}\,location + b_{3}\,gender*location + e$?
4. Why does a small effect need so many more participants than a large one?
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. The dark blue curve crosses the line of 0.8 at about 25 participants per group. The exact value is `r n_per_group_needed[["large (d = 0.8)"]]` per group, so `r 2 * n_per_group_needed[["large (d = 0.8)"]]` in total.
2. With 20 participants per group, the medium blue curve is at about 0.3: the exact power is `r format_number(power_20_per_group)`. The study would miss an effect of this size `r round(100 * (1 - power_20_per_group))` times out of 100. Advise the student to recruit at least `r n_per_group_needed[["medium (d = 0.5)"]]` participants per group, or to change the design.
3. $gender$ has 1 df (2 categories - 1), $location$ has 2 df (3 categories - 1) and the interaction has $1 \times 2 = 2$ df. The Numerator df is $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$.
4. A small difference between two groups is hidden by the variability of the observations. Only a large sample makes the estimate precise enough to tell it apart from 0. As @sec-lecture-04 says, the significance of an estimate depends on the strength of the relationship and on the sample size.
:::

::: {#exr-l06-scenarios}
## $p$-hacking, $p$-HARKing or fine?

Say whether each practice is $p$-hacking, $p$-HARKing or fine, and why.

a. A researcher tests the effect of $salary$ on $js\_score$. It is not significant, so she tests $perf$, then $gender$, then $location$, each in its own model, and reports only the significant one.
b. A researcher finds by chance that $location$ predicts $js\_score$. In the paper, the introduction announces this effect as the hypothesis of the study.
c. A researcher pre-registers three hypotheses on the open science framework, tests them in one model, and reports all the results, significant or not.
d. A researcher builds a correlation table of 10 variables and reports every correlation with $p < .05$ as a finding.
e. A researcher notices an unexpected effect, reports it as an exploratory result, and tests it again on new data.
:::

```{r}
#| label: exercise-scenarios
#| include: false
correlations_10_variables <- choose(10, 2)
risk_10_variables <- 1 - 0.95^correlations_10_variables
```

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
a. **$p$-hacking.** The tests are run until a significant $p$-value appears, with one test by hypothesis instead of one unique test. With four tests, the risk of at least one false positive would already be `r scales::percent(1 - 0.95^4, accuracy = 1)` if the tests were independent (@fig-l06-false-positives).
b. **$p$-HARKing.** A post hoc hypothesis, based on the results, is presented as if it were an a priori hypothesis.
c. **Fine.** This is the good practice of the chapter: pre-registration, one model for all the hypotheses and a full report.
d. **$p$-hacking.** A table of 10 variables holds `r correlations_10_variables` correlations. If none of them existed in the population, the risk of at least one false positive would be $1 - 0.95^{`r correlations_10_variables`} = `r format_number(risk_10_variables)`$, that is `r scales::percent(risk_10_variables, accuracy = 1)`, if the tests were independent. $p$-values are produced only to test hypotheses formulated beforehand (@sec-lecture-04).
e. **Fine.** The result is presented for what it is, and the new test is done on new data.
:::

```{r}
#| label: exercise-comparison
#| include: false
comparison_interaction <- anova(model_additive, model_interaction)
aic_additive <- AIC(model_additive)
aic_interaction <- AIC(model_interaction)
```

::: {#exr-l06-comparison}
## Is the interaction useful?

Open `organisation_beta.csv` in jamovi (or in R) and answer the "Your turn" question of @sec-l06-comparison-jamovi: compare the full model $js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,salary + b_{2}\,perf + b_{3}\,salary*perf + e$ with the simple model $js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,salary + b_{2}\,perf + e$.

1. Which model has the smaller $AIC$?
2. Is the difference between the two models statistically significant?
3. Write one sentence for the results section.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In jamovi, set $js\_score$ as the Dependent Variable and $salary$ and $perf$ as Covariates. In the Model Builder, put $salary$ and $perf$ in Block 1. Add a New Block and bring the interaction $salary*perf$ into Block 2 (select both variables at once). Tick $AIC$ in the Model Fit options.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "R code"
model_additive <- lm(js_score ~ salary + perf, data = organisation_beta)
model_interaction <- lm(js_score ~ salary * perf, data = organisation_beta)
anova(model_additive, model_interaction)
AIC(model_additive, model_interaction)
```

1. The simple model: $AIC = `r format_number(aic_additive)`$ without the interaction and $AIC = `r format_number(aic_interaction)`$ with it.
2. No. The comparison gives $F(`r comparison_interaction$Df[2]`, `r comparison_interaction$Res.Df[2]`) = `r format_number(comparison_interaction$F[2])`$, $`r format_p(comparison_interaction$"Pr(>F)"[2])`$. Adding the interaction does not improve the accuracy of the model.
3. Adding the interaction between $salary$ and $perf$ did not significantly improve the predictions of the model ($F(`r comparison_interaction$Df[2]`, `r comparison_interaction$Res.Df[2]`) = `r format_number(comparison_interaction$F[2])`$, $`r format_p(comparison_interaction$"Pr(>F)"[2])`$), and it increased the $AIC$ from `r format_number(aic_additive)` to `r format_number(aic_interaction)`.
:::

#| label: exercise-assumptions-perf
#| include: false
cook_perf <- cooks.distance(model_perf)
studentised_perf <- rstudent(model_perf)
employee_largest_cook_perf <- organisation_beta$employee[which.max(cook_perf)]

::: {#exr-l06-assumptions}
## Checking and reporting the assumptions

Take the model of the first "Your turn" box of this chapter, $js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,perf + e$.

1. In jamovi (or in R), check the four assumptions and look for anomalous data.
2. Write the sentences that report these checks in a results section.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In jamovi, run the Linear Regression with $js\_score$ as the Dependent Variable and $perf$ as a Covariate, open **Assumption Checks** and tick all the boxes. Plot $js\_score$ against $perf$ to check linearity.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "R code"
model_perf <- lm(js_score ~ perf, data = organisation_beta)
# Linearity: the outcome against the predictor
plot(js_score ~ perf, data = organisation_beta)
# Normality: the Q-Q plot of the residuals
plot(model_perf, which = 2)
# Equal variance: the residuals against the fitted values
plot(model_perf, which = 1)
# Anomalous data
summary(cooks.distance(model_perf))
range(rstudent(model_perf))
```

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Two plots for the model of js_score on perf. Left, a Q-Q plot of the standardised residuals: the 20 points lie close to the blue line. Right, the residuals against the fitted values: the fitted values only go from about 6.77 to 6.87 and the points form a cloud with no funnel and no curve."
#| fig-height: 3
perf_checks <- tibble(
  fitted = fitted(model_perf),
  residual = residuals(model_perf),
  standardised = rstandard(model_perf)
)

plot_qq_perf <- ggplot(perf_checks, aes(sample = standardised)) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = book_col("blue"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  stat_qq(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Standardised residuals")

plot_residuals_perf <- ggplot(perf_checks, aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = book_col("grey"), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")

plot_qq_perf + plot_residuals_perf
```

1. The four assumptions and the anomalous data:
    - **Linearity.** The scatterplot of $js\_score$ against $perf$ shows no curve: the points are spread around an almost flat line.
    - **Independence.** Each employee gives one observation, and the data were simulated independently for each employee (@sec-lecture-04). Nothing suggests that two observations are related.
    - **Normality.** In the Q-Q plot, the points stay close to the line.
    - **Equal variance.** The residual plot shows a cloud of points with no funnel. The fitted values vary very little, because $perf$ hardly predicts $js\_score$.
    - **Anomalous data.** The studentised residuals go from `r format_number(min(studentised_perf))` to `r format_number(max(studentised_perf))`, none beyond +3 or -3. The maximum Cook's distance is `r format_number(max(cook_perf))` (employee `r employee_largest_cook_perf`) and the mean is `r format_number(mean(cook_perf))`, far below 1.
2. A possible report: "The assumptions of the model were checked. The relationship between $perf$ and $js\_score$ showed no curve, the Q-Q plot of the residuals showed points close to the line, and the plot of the residuals against the fitted values showed no pattern. No observation was an outlier (all studentised residuals between -3 and 3) and none had a high influence (maximum Cook's distance = `r format_number(max(cook_perf))`, mean = `r format_number(mean(cook_perf))`)."
:::

```{r}
#| label: exercise-agent
#| include: false
salary_p <- summary(model_salary)$coefficients["salary", "Pr(>|t|)"]
perf_p <- summary(model_perf)$coefficients["perf", "Pr(>|t|)"]
vif_reported <- vif_additive
```

::: {#exr-l06-agent}
## Checking the work of an AI agent

A student asks an AI agent to test two hypotheses on the Organisation Beta data in jamovi Cloud, $H_{a1}$ ($salary$ increases $js\_score$) and $H_{a2}$ ($perf$ increases $js\_score$). The agent returns this text. Find at least five problems.

> I ran two regressions: one of $js\_score$ on $salary$ and one of $js\_score$ on $perf$. The variable $js\_score$ is normally distributed, so the normality assumption is met. The VIF is `r format_number(vif_reported)`, so there are no outliers. Employee 7 has a studentised residual of `r format_number(employee_7$studentised)`, so I removed this employee. The effect of $salary$ is significant ($`r format_p(salary_p)`$) and the effect of $perf$ is not ($`r format_p(perf_p)`$), so $H_{a2}$ is rejected.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
- **Two models instead of one.** The hypotheses should be tested in one unique model, $js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,salary + b_{2}\,perf + e$, not with one test by hypothesis (@sec-l06-badgood).
- **Normality of the wrong variable.** The assumption is about the residuals, not about $js\_score$.
- **The VIF says nothing about outliers.** It measures collinearity between predictors. Outliers are found with the studentised residuals, and influence with Cook's distance. Besides, a model with one predictor has no VIF: the value comes from the model with both predictors.
- **An outlier removed without reason.** Employee 7 is an outlier, but the Cook's distance of this employee is `r format_number(employee_7$cook)`, far below 1. Removing it changes the data until the model fits. It must stay, unless the data of employee 7 turn out to be junk data.
- **A wrong conclusion.** A non-significant effect does not reject $H_{a2}$: $H_{0_{2}}$ can't be rejected (@sec-lecture-04).
- **An incomplete report.** The fit of the model ($R^2$, $F$, $p$) and, for each estimate, $b$, its 95% confidence interval and $t$ are missing. These are the checks that @sec-l06-whatai asks you to make on the work of an AI.
:::
